PRIVATE BY DEFAULT / NO SIGN-UP

Find the tenders worth your time.

Paste a public tender CSV, filter it to your trade and minimum contract value, and get a deadline-ordered shortlist. Your listings stay in this browser.

Build a shortlist

Add a CSV export to begin.

DeadlineDays leftTitleBuyerCategoryValueSource

What this does not do

It does not decide whether you are eligible, verify a notice, predict your chance of winning, or submit a bid. Use the shortlist as a review aid and check the original portal before relying on any detail.

Common questions

What CSV format does it expect?

Columns named title, buyer, deadline, category, value, url, with deadline as a sortable date string like 2026-09-18 and value as a plain number. Most tender portals export something close to this; if a column is named differently, rename the header row in your CSV before pasting it in, since the parser matches on those exact names.

Does the category filter understand synonyms, like “roofing” matching “roof repair”?

Type a comma-separated list — roofing, roof repair, reroof — and a row matches if any term appears in its category or title. It is still a plain text match, not a trade taxonomy or a fuzzy search, so a spelling you did not list (“re-roofing” with a hyphen, say) still needs adding by hand. This replaced an earlier version that only took one term and made you re-run the filter per spelling.

Does this tell me if I'm eligible to bid or improve my odds of winning?

No — as the section above states, it does not decide eligibility, verify a notice, predict your chance of winning, or submit a bid. It only sorts and filters a CSV you already have to a deadline-ordered shortlist; treat every row as something to confirm against the original portal.

Is my tender list uploaded anywhere?

No. Parsing and filtering happen entirely in your browser; listings are never uploaded, and there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Only anonymous local usage counts are kept, and you can turn that off with the button in the footer.

Does it remember my pasted CSV if I close the tab?

Yes. Your pasted CSV and filter settings are saved to this browser's local storage after you create a shortlist, and are restored the next time you open the page -- so a workflow you use every week doesn't start from a blank textarea each time. Nothing is saved anywhere but this browser. Use "Clear saved data" to remove it.

← Tender Radar

Tender Radar vs. GovWin IQ

Two different jobs: GovWin IQ, from Deltek, is an account-based platform for finding public-sector opportunities and tracking who else bids on them. Tender Radar is a free, private browser tool for a narrower job — turning a CSV export you already have into a deadline-ordered shortlist, before you spend an afternoon reading notices that were never going to fit your trade or your floor value.

Open the free tender shortlist tool

What each tool is for

GovWin IQ is a government-contracting intelligence platform built by Deltek for contractors who sell into the public sector: opportunity discovery and forecasting, incumbent and competitor tracking, and agency spending history, run as an ongoing account. GovWin IQ's own pricing and current feature list are not reachable from this session to confirm, so no dollar figure or plan name for GovWin IQ is stated here — only its well-documented identity and category, an account-based public-sector opportunity and competitive-intelligence platform.

Tender Radar does none of what GovWin IQ does. It does not find opportunities, forecast agency spending, or track competitors. It takes a CSV export you already have — title, buyer, deadline, category, value, url — and filters it by trade (matching several spellings of the same trade in one pass), a minimum contract value, and deadline runway, entirely in your browser, with no account and nothing uploaded. Your pasted CSV and filter settings are saved to your own browser's local storage so the shortlist workflow is there again next time you open the page.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
I need to find public-sector opportunities and see who else usually bids on them.GovWin IQ, or a comparable platform — opportunity discovery is not something Tender Radar does.
I already have a list of notices. Which ones are actually worth reading closely?Tender Radar — free, instant, private, no account.
The same trade is spelled three different ways across my export. Can I catch all of them in one filter?Tender Radar's trade filter takes a comma-separated list of spellings and matches any of them.
How has this agency awarded similar contracts in the past?GovWin IQ, or a comparable research platform — Tender Radar only sorts and filters the export you give it.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?Tender Radar: no. GovWin IQ is used through a Deltek account.

Most public-sector contractors get different value from each: GovWin IQ (or a comparable platform) for finding and forecasting opportunities as an ongoing account, and a private tool like Tender Radar for cutting a CSV export — from that platform or any portal — down to a deadline-ordered shortlist in minutes. Once a notice survives the shortlist, the bid readiness checker covers the paperwork go/no-go on it; Tender Radar's own findings are a shortlist, not a market forecast or a competitor record.

Common questions

Should I use Tender Radar or GovWin IQ?

Often both, for different jobs. GovWin IQ, from Deltek, is a government-contracting intelligence platform for finding public-sector opportunities and tracking agency and competitor history, run as an ongoing account. Tender Radar does none of that. It takes a CSV export of notices you already have — from a portal, from GovWin IQ, or from anywhere else — and filters it by trade, minimum value, and deadline into a shortlist you can read in minutes, entirely in your browser, with no account and nothing uploaded. A contractor who needs to discover and forecast public-sector opportunities is better served by GovWin IQ or a comparable platform; a contractor who already has a list of notices and wants it cut down to what is worth an afternoon is in the right place here.

Does GovWin IQ filter a tender list by trade, value, and deadline the way Tender Radar does?

GovWin IQ's own search and saved-opportunity tooling can narrow what it surfaces, but turning an arbitrary CSV export you already hold into a fast, private, deadline-ordered shortlist is not that platform's job any more than opportunity discovery and agency-spending research are Tender Radar's job. Some contractors use GovWin IQ or a comparable service to find and export notices, then run that export through Tender Radar before reading any of them closely; neither tool replaces the other.

which-tenders-are-worth-bidding-on.html.text:
← Tender Radar

Which public tenders are worth bidding on?

A tender portal's default view is not a pipeline. It is every notice the authority published this week, sorted by the date it went up, in categories the buyer chose rather than the ones you work in. Reading it end to end is an afternoon, and most of that afternoon is spent on contracts in the wrong trade, below the value where bidding pays, or closing on Thursday.

Three filters remove almost all of it.

Open the free tender shortlist tool

Filter one: your trade, spelled every way buyers spell it

This is the filter that quietly loses work. Public buyers write their own titles and pick their own category labels, so the same job is roofing at one authority, roof repair at the next, and reroof at the third. A one-word search finds a third of your market and tells you the market is thin.

The fix is to filter on a comma-separated list of the words your trade actually goes by — roofing, roof repair, reroof — and match a row if any of them appears in its category or its title. It stays a plain substring match rather than a synonym dictionary, so a spelling you did not think of is still missed. Adding one when you notice it costs nothing.

Filter two: a floor value

Every bid costs roughly the same to assemble whether the contract is $12,000 or $120,000: the same bonds, the same insurance evidence, the same declarations, the same day of estimating. Below some value that effort cannot be recovered even by winning. Set that floor explicitly and let the filter enforce it, rather than deciding case by case at the end of a long list when the marginal notice always looks tempting.

Filter three: deadline runway

Sort what is left by deadline and read from the top. A contract you would win, closing in three days, with a bond you do not yet have, is not an opportunity — and it is much easier to see that when the shortlist is ordered by the clock rather than by publication date.

Worked example

A roofing contractor filters an export on roofing, roof repair, reroof with a minimum value of 20,000. A school roof replacement and a clinic reroof survive. A $12,000 painting hall — which the portal had filed under a category the contractor's single-word search would also have matched — drops out on value. Two listings to read properly, in deadline order, instead of ninety.

What it does not do

The tool filters a CSV you export yourself (title, buyer, deadline, category, value, url), entirely in your browser. Nothing is uploaded. It does not connect to portals, monitor them, submit bids, or offer eligibility advice — verify every listing, requirement, deadline, and declaration at the original source before acting. Once you have a shortlist, the bid readiness checker covers the paperwork go/no-go on each one.

Common questions

How do I find public tenders worth bidding on?

Export the notices from the portal you already have access to, then filter them on three things before reading any of them: whether the trade matches what you do, whether the contract value clears the floor below which the bid effort is not worth it, and whether the deadline leaves enough runway to assemble a compliant submission. What survives all three is a shortlist worth an afternoon; the rest is a portal's default view, which is not a pipeline.

Why does one trade need several search terms?

Public buyers write their own titles and pick their own categories, so the same work appears as 'roofing', 'roof repair', and 'reroof' across three notices from three authorities. A single-word filter silently drops the other two. Filtering on a comma-separated list of the words your trade is actually called catches all of them in one pass — but it is a plain substring match, not a synonym dictionary, so a spelling you did not list is still missed.

Does this tool fetch tenders from portals for me?

No. It filters a CSV you export yourself, entirely in your browser, and nothing is uploaded. It does not connect to portals, submit bids, or judge whether you are eligible. Verify every listing, requirement, deadline, and declaration against the original source before acting on it.
